Vignette:
# Kavi's Vigil (Complete)

Kavi Perera was forty-one when the convoy was ambushed near Kandahar. He had been flying transport helicopters for the Australian Defence Force for eight years by then, and he had come to understand the work as a kind of calling—moving supplies, moving people, moving hope into places where it was needed. The morning of the attack, he was waiting on the tarmac for clearance, the rotors already turning, when the radio crackled with a request for emergency extraction from a forward operating base. Three soldiers had been hit. He lifted off without hesitation. The landing zone was chaos. Dust everywhere, the smell of cordite and something else—something burnt that he would later learn was human tissue. One of the injured men was conscious, his uniform soaked through with blood, and as Kavi's crew loaded him aboard, the man's hand—cold, trembling—grabbed Kavi's wrist. The texture of it stays with him still: the particular roughness of a field dressing soaked through, the specific way a dying man's grip feels when he is trying not to let go of the world. They got airborne. They did not make it to the hospital. The man died in the cabin while Kavi was flying, and for the last thirty seconds of that flight, Kavi had felt the weight of that hand on his wrist even though someone had already pried the fingers away. He had felt the man's blood cooling against his skin. In the years that followed, Kavi would learn to live with the memory as though it belonged to someone else entirely—a different man in a different life, someone he could observe from a distance but never quite become again. Yet when that memory surfaced, which it did without warning and without mercy, it carried the full weight of the original terror, as if twenty-two years had collapsed into nothing.

Now, at sixty-three, Kavi flies for a major American carrier as a captain on long-haul routes, a position he has held for the last decade. He and his wife Margaret live in Portland, and to anyone watching him move through an airport or into the cockpit, he appears composed—professional, even. But Kavi has come to understand that he is not the man who boarded that helicopter in 2002. That man is gone, and what remains is something he has come to regard with a kind of horror. The night vigilance started years ago, so gradually that he did not notice it at first. He would wake at 2:47 a.m.—the exact time the convoy was hit—and lie in the dark, listening. Margaret would be asleep beside him, and he would feel the house around him like a trap, every door and window a potential breach. He had come to believe that darkness was the time when things became real, when the world showed its true nature. During the day, the illusion of safety held. At night, it fell away. The scanning began during his first year with the American airline. He would enter a cockpit or a briefing room and immediately locate the exits—not consciously, but as an automatic sweep of his eyes before he could attend to anything else. In the cabin, waiting for a flight to board, he would map the space, note where people stood, anticipate sudden movements. When a flight attendant moved too quickly, or when a passenger stood abruptly, Kavi's body would tense, his breath would catch. He was certain that everyone was a potential threat, though he could not articulate why. The world had shown him its teeth once, and he had never stopped waiting for them to close.

The memory itself has become something alien to him—something that belongs to a different person, a different life. When it surfaces, which it does without warning and without mercy, it carries with it the full weight of that original terror, as vivid as the moment it happened. A particular texture—canvas, or certain kinds of fabric, or even the specific roughness of the armrest in the cockpit—can trigger it instantly. The sound of a helicopter, even on television, can send him into a state where he is back on that tarmac, feeling that cold grip on his wrist. The time of day matters too. As 2:47 a.m. approaches, his body knows, and he lies awake, waiting for the moment when something inside him will fracture again. The sight of blood—even in a medical context, even in a film—can leave him shaking for hours afterward. He has come to believe that his mind is fundamentally unreliable, that the boundary between past and present has become dangerously thin, and that this defect marks him as someone who should not be trusted with the lives of three hundred passengers on every flight he captains.

Margaret has noticed the changes. She has watched him become someone who is always miserable, who moves through their marriage like a man underwater. He used to laugh easily. He used to be present. Now he is elsewhere, always scanning, always vigilant. She has noticed that he no longer touches her at night, that he flinches when she reaches for him in the dark, that he sometimes calls her by the name of a crew member from a flight years ago. The airline has not noticed yet, but Kavi knows they will. He has started making mistakes, small ones, the kind that come from a mind that is never quite here. Last month, during a preflight checklist, he found himself unable to remember whether he had already verified the fuel levels, and the uncertainty terrified him in a way that no threat assessment ever could. He began a descent procedure and had to abort it halfway through because he could not recall if he had already completed it. The fear that he might one day forget something critical—that his mind might betray him in a moment that matters—has become more terrifying than any external threat. It was Margaret who finally insisted he come. She said she could not bear to watch him disappear anymore, and Kavi, sitting in the therapist's office now, can only agree. He does not know if anything can fix what he is, but he has run out of ways to hide it. What frightens him most is not that he will remember the dying soldier's grip—he will, always—but that he will forget something that costs lives, and that the defect inside him will finally be exposed for what it is: a fundamental failure of the person he has tried so hard to remain.

missing_items: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person
Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
missing_explanations: While the vignette extensively describes Kavi's belief that his mind is 'fundamentally unreliable' and his fear of being a 'defect,' this is framed as cognitive/memory dysfunction rather than a core personal defectiveness. The negative appraisal 'There is something wrong with me as a person' is not directly articulated as a general character flaw.

The vignette states 'he has watched him become someone who is always miserable' and references his loss of happiness ('He used to laugh easily'), which does reflect this symptom. However, this appears only in Margaret's observations rather than as Kavi's own self-reported experience or internal narrative.

While the vignette emphasizes Kavi's belief that 'The world had shown him its teeth' and his sense of threat, the specific appraisal 'The world is a dangerous place' as a generalized belief about the world is not explicitly stated. His threat responses are triggered-specific (scanning, vigilance at night) rather than a broad philosophical conviction that the world itself is inherently dangerous.
